options: A JSON record mapping each resource in your config to its real-world ID and attributes
A log of every terraform command ever run
A backup copy of your .tf source files
A compiled binary of your Terraform configuration
questions.explain: State is how Terraform knows what already exists, so plan can diff reality against config instead of guessing.

questions.q: With no backend block configured anywhere in a Terraform project, where does terraform.tfstate get written?
options: To the Terraform Registry
To the local backend — the current working directory on whichever machine ran the command
Automatically to a shared Terraform Cloud workspace
Nowhere; Terraform refuses to run without a backend block
questions.explain: No backend block means Terraform defaults to the local backend, writing state to disk wherever you ran terraform apply.

questions.q: A teammate checks out your Terraform config but has no copy of your terraform.tfstate. What happens when they run terraform plan?
options: Terraform sees zero known resources and plans to create everything, even though the infrastructure already exists
Terraform refuses to run and prints an error
Terraform automatically downloads the correct state from your laptop
Terraform silently skips the plan step
questions.explain: With no shared source of truth, Terraform has no record of what already exists, so it plans as if nothing does.

questions.q: Why is committing terraform.tfstate to a git repository a real security problem?
options: State routinely contains passwords, keys, and connection strings in plain text, and git history is hard to fully scrub
Git has a hard file-size limit that state files always exceed
It is not actually a problem as long as the repo is private
State files are encrypted and git cannot store encrypted files
questions.explain: Sensitive values land in state unencrypted regardless of how they were marked in config, so committing it exposes them permanently.

questions.q: Why can't two teammates safely run terraform apply at nearly the same time against local state?
options: Local state files are read-only after the first apply
Each apply creates a brand-new state file, so there's no conflict
Local state has no locking mechanism, so concurrent writes can overwrite or corrupt the same file
Terraform always queues applies automatically, so this is never actually a risk
questions.explain: Without a shared, lockable backend, nothing stops two simultaneous writes to the same state file from colliding.
